claim: This finding from the previous review no longer holds at the reviewed head: The catalog rewrite in `src/sqllens/safety/rule_sets.py` (lines 267-275 and 402-403) turns a reference to `information_schema.TABLES`, `COLUMNS` or `KEY_COLUMN_USAGE` into a derived table whose inner source is a real table node named `TABLES`, `COLUMNS` or `KEY_COLUMN_USAGE`. Before this change those statements were refused outright, so they never reached the inner runners; now the rewritten SQL passes through `RlsGuardRunner`, and `apply_rls` in `src/sqllens/safety/rls.py` (lines 271-282) keys its rules on `table.name.lower()` alone and ignores the schema qualifier. In a deployment that configures both a rule-set file and an `[[rls]]` rule for an application table named `tables`, `columns` or `key_column_usage`, that rule's predicate is injected into the guard-built catalog body, and MySQL rejects the statement because the predicate's column does not exist in the catalog view. The model's only schema-lookup path then fails on every attempt. The predicate only narrows rows, so this is breakage rather than a data leak, and no unit or connector test pairs a rule set with a name-colliding row-security rule. (raised by 1/6 agents)

The predicate only narrows rows, so this is breakage rather than a data leak, and no unit or connector test pairs a rule set with a name-colliding row-security rule. (raised by 1/6 agents)
